title: Incident Response Process
summary: The lifecycle of a security incident from detection through post-incident review.
content:
# Incident Response Process

## Purpose
This document defines how a security incident is handled from first detection to closure. It
follows the NIST 800-61 phases: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication
and recovery, and post-incident activity.

## Detection and analysis
An incident begins when an analyst confirms that an alert or report represents a genuine
security event. Open an incident record immediately, even while facts are thin - the record is
where the timeline accumulates, and reconstructing one after the fact is much harder.

Assign severity from impact and scope, not from how alarming the alert looked. Critical means
active compromise of production systems or confirmed exfiltration of sensitive data. High
means confirmed compromise of a single system, or credible attempted compromise of critical
infrastructure. Medium means suspicious activity requiring investigation with no confirmed
compromise. Low means policy violations and minor issues.

Record what you know and what you are assuming, and keep those separate.

## Containment
Contain before you investigate deeply. Short-term containment stops the immediate damage -
isolate the affected host from the network, block the hostile address, disable the compromised
account. Preserve evidence while doing so: capture volatile memory before powering anything
off, and take a disk image before rebuilding.

Long-term containment keeps the business running while eradication is planned: temporary
firewall rules, elevated monitoring, tightened access.

## Eradication and recovery
Remove the attacker access and the vulnerability that admitted them. Rotate every credential
the attacker could have obtained. Rebuild compromised hosts from known-good images rather
than cleaning them in place; a cleaned host you cannot fully account for is a host you do not
trust.

Restore service in stages, monitoring for the return of the attacker. Do not close the
incident at the moment service is restored - watch first.

## Communication
Notify the incident commander for any high or critical incident. Legal and communications
teams engage where personal data or regulatory obligations are involved, and their timelines
often start at the moment of discovery. Keep a decision log: who decided what, when, and on
what evidence.

## Post-incident review
Within two weeks of closure, hold a blameless review. Establish the timeline, the root cause,
what worked and what did not, and what would have detected this sooner. Produce concrete
actions with owners and dates. An incident that produces no change to detection, prevention or
process has been wasted.
